title: What Is Motorola DynaTAC 8000X? — Definition
body:
The telephone converts voice to electrical signals and back, and the telephone network switches those signals between any two subscribers. From Bell's 1876 patent through candlestick phones, rotary dials, Strowger and crossbar exchanges, touch-tone DTMF, and the first mobile systems, this category covers a century of wired and early wireless voice before the smartphone.

In the context of this database, the Motorola DynaTAC 8000X is presented as one telephone record among the telephone history family. The brick: $3,995, 2 lbs, 30 minutes of talk — Martin Cooper's 1973 demo made real.

title: Origins and History of Motorola DynaTAC 8000X
body:
The Motorola DynaTAC 8000X belongs to the 1983–1994 era and traces to Motorola.

Bell's 1876 patent (filed hours before Elisha Gray's caveat) launched the telephone; by 1878 New Haven had the first exchange. Candlestick and wall phones with separate receivers gave way to the Western Electric 302 (1937) — the iconic desk phone. Automatic switching (Strowger, 1891) replaced 'hello girls'; panel and crossbar systems scaled cities. The 1951 transistor and 1960s ESS electronic switching digitized the core. Touch-tone (1963) replaced rotary pulse dialing; the 1984 Bell breakup deregulated the US. Meanwhile mobile telephony grew from MTS car phones (1946) through IMTS to AMPS cellular (1983) — the 1G era that made the brick phone possible.

Within that longer story, Motorola DynaTAC 8000X: The first commercial handheld cellular phone; the yuppie icon. FCC approval 1983; the mobile era's big bang.

title: How Motorola DynaTAC 8000X Works
body:
A carbon microphone varies resistance with sound pressure, modulating line current; at the far end an electromagnetic receiver turns current back into sound. Rotary dials pulse the line (1–10 breaks); DTMF sends pairs of tones. Exchanges connect lines: Strowger step-by-step switches climbed banks of contacts; crossbar used matrices of magnets; ESS stored programs did it in software. Long-distance rode open wire, then coaxial, then microwave relay, then fiber. Cellular divides territory into cells reusing frequencies, handing calls off as you move.

Applied to the Motorola DynaTAC 8000X (1983–1994, Motorola): FCC approval 1983; the mobile era's big bang.

title: Anatomy of Motorola DynaTAC 8000X — Components
body:
Every Motorola DynaTAC 8000X is an assembly of the telephone history family's standard parts:

• Carbon transmitter — Granule microphone; the voice of telephony for 80 years.
• Receiver — Electromagnetic earpiece; later dynamic and balanced-armature.
• Induction coil — Hybrid transformer separating transmit/receive (sidetone).
• Rotary dial — Spring-governed pulse mechanism; 10 pps.
• DTMF pad — 12/16-key tone generator; 697–1633 Hz pairs.
• Ringer — Biased bell with clapper; 20 Hz 90 V ringing signal.
• Line switch / hookswitch — On/off-hook detection starting everything.
• Exchange switch — Strowger, panel, crossbar, or ESS fabric.
• Loading coils — Inductors extending voice frequency range on long loops.
• Repeater — Amplifier (tube, then transistor) for long-haul circuits.

When examining a surviving Motorola DynaTAC 8000X, identify these parts in order: Carbon transmitter, Receiver, Induction coil, Rotary dial, DTMF pad, Ringer.

title: Telephone History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of telephone history:

• POTS — Plain Old Telephone Service; the analog copper network.
• loop — The two-wire circuit from exchange to subscriber.
• off-hook / on-hook — Line states; everything keys off the hookswitch.
• dial tone — 350+440 Hz: the network saying 'ready'.
• DTMF — Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency; Touch-Tone dialing.
• pulse dialing — Rotary interruptions: 1 pulse per digit.
• party line — Shared line; ring codes identified the household.
• trunk — High-capacity link between exchanges.
• exchange / central office — The building where lines switch.
• area code — 1947 NANP routing zones; 201 New Jersey was first.
• 1A2 key system — Multi-line office phones with hold buttons.
• cord board — Manual switchboard with plug cords; 'number please'.

title: Motorola DynaTAC 8000X Restoration Guide
body:
Replace cloth cords and cracked housings; clean dial mechanisms and oil sparingly. Convert to modular jacks with proper polarity. Test ringers on a real 90V source, not a 9V battery. Never connect unrestored phones to live VoIP adapters without checking REN load.

Restoration order for a Motorola DynaTAC 8000X: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical telephone record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: Motorola DynaTAC 8000X — DTMF tone math + rotary pulse timing (Runnable Python)
body:
Computes the exact DTMF tone pairs for any digit and simulates rotary-dial pulse trains — the two dialing languages of the wired century.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Motorola DynaTAC 8000X so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# DTMF pairs + rotary pulse timing (public-domain telephony math)
ROWS = [697, 770, 852, 941]
COLS = [1209, 1336, 1477, 1633]
KEYS = [["1","2","3","A"],["4","5","6","B"],["7","8","9","C"],["*","0","#","D"]]

def dtmf(digit):
    for r, row in enumerate(KEYS):
        for c, k in enumerate(row):
            if k == digit:
                return ROWS[r], COLS[c]
    return None

number = "555-0199"
print("DTMF dialing", number)
for d in number:
    if d == "-": print("  pause"); continue
    print(f"  {d}: {dtmf(d)[0]} Hz + {dtmf(d)[1]} Hz")

# Rotary: digit N -> N pulses at 10 pps, 60% break / 40% make, 600ms+ inter-digit
def rotary_time(number):
    t = 0.0
    for d in number:
        if d == "-": t += 0.6; continue
        n = 10 if d == "0" else int(d)
        t += n * 0.1 + 0.6   # pulses + inter-digit pause
    return t
print(f"\nRotary dialing {number} takes ~{rotary_time(number):.1f} seconds")
demo_title: DTMF tone math + rotary pulse timing
